Series::copysign¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::copysign(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::copysign_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::copysign_(const Series& rhs) const

What It Does¶

copysign() builds a value from the magnitude of the receiver a and the sign of other b:

copysign(a, b) = |a| * sign(b)

So copysign(5, -3) is -5, and copysign(-5, 3) is 5. The magnitude of b is irrelevant; only whether b is positive or negative (including the sign of a zero) matters.

This is the tool for “give me x but pointing the same way as y” without a branch — reflecting a step to move toward a target, matching the orientation of a normal vector, or restoring a sign that was stripped by an abs().

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The sign source b. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& |a| carrying the sign of b. Integer inputs stay integer. copysign_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

copysign() is differentiable in the receiver only:

d/da copysign(a, b) = sign(a) * sign(b)
d/db copysign(a, b) = 0

The receiver’s gradient is +1 when a and b already share a sign and -1 when they differ (that is exactly the factor that maps a to |a| * sign(b)). b contributes only its sign bit, which carries no usable derivative, so its gradient is 0.

In-Place Form¶

copysign_() is the in-place sibling of copysign(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — copysign_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({3.0, -3.0}, {2});
auto y = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 1.0}, {2});

x.copysign_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-3, 3]

Examples¶

Example 1. Magnitude from a, sign from b.

auto a = pluss::make_series({5.0, -5.0, 5.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({-3.0, 3.0, 0.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.copysign(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-5.0000, 5.0000, 5.0000]

A positive-zero b counts as a positive sign, so the third result is +5.

Example 2. Integer inputs stay integer.

auto a = pluss::make_series({5, -5, 5}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
auto b = pluss::make_series({-1, 1, -1}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.copysign(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-5, 5, -5]

Example 3. The gradient flows only to the magnitude source, with sign sign(a) * sign(b).

auto a = pluss::make_series({5.0, -5.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({-3.0, 3.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.copysign(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0]

For (a = 5, b = -3) the output is -5, so the derivative wrt a is -1. For (a = -5, b = 3) the output is 5, again -1. b gets nothing.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The magnitude of other is ignored. copysign(5, -0.001) and copysign(5, -1000) both give -5.

  • The sign of a zero in other matters: +0.0 is a positive sign, -0.0 is negative.

  • b receives no gradient. If you need the target’s value to influence training, copysign() is the wrong op.

  • NaN in a propagates as NaN with b’s sign; a NaN in b has a platform-defined sign bit.

Summary¶

copysign(a, b) is |a| wearing the sign of b:

  • broadcasts like add(); preserves integer dtype

  • only the sign of b is read, not its magnitude

  • differentiable in a (gradient sign(a) * sign(b)), zero in b

See Also¶

  • Series::abs: drop the sign; copysign() is how you put one back.

  • Series::sign: extract just the sign as -1 / 0 / +1.

  • Series::mul: if you want the magnitude of b to matter too.
